I've tinkered with an arduino a while back and found it was quite easy to get something up and running (in my case a temperature controller fan). My initial plan was to get things up and running on the arduino and a bread board, and then create a custom board with an ATmega chip. But eventually I ended up leaving the arduino nano in the final project.

I found that there is a big difference in programming the arduino and programming a new ATmega. I'm now trying to learn how to use AtmelStudio and feel like I'm unlearning a lot of the shortcuts ardunio uses.

I can see that arduino has a place for the casual hobbyist, but I question whether it's really that good for students to be learning if they plan to pursue this more professionally.

That being said, I tried using an ARM development board and really struggled. So for now I plan to give ATmegas another go and hopefully learn the basics from there. Do you think this is this the best way to learn embedded hardware?
Is arduino a good starting point for someone looking to get into embedded hardware?

The fact that you could get a project up and running relatively easy is beneficial I think.

I started with Basic Stamp ICs (before Arduino was a thing) and later used Phidget modules (I seem to remember using Visual Studio to program these?). Arduino is an improvement on both, but essentially the same concept.

I would argue that Arduinos are more beneficial to software developers. It gets them up and running very fast without having to really learn much hardware.

For someone like yourself who wants to learn hardware, taking shortcuts and skipping the fundamentals really only postpones learning all that until later. You're still going to need to learn this as you're finding out now. I think 8-bit AVRs are a good choice, but I'd also suggest brushing up on electronics fundamentals if required. Are you currently a student?

I'd like to add a bit more info to the answer of /u/mash_taiters. It always depends on what you want to focus on. If you want to make embedded systems that perform non critical operations, and simple applications (i.e. a meteorological station) then with the arduino and the very basics of electronics you should be OK. If you want to design more complicated or critical systems, then you will need a good book that introduce you to the concepts of the micro controllers, a deeper knowledge of electronics etc. While reading these books, I'd recommend you to program applications using the API that comes with the Arduino, and then try to substitute some of those API calls with your own methods. After all, the Arduino has an Atmel chip inside, so you can test your knowledge with it. You can start by programming a GPIO pin to be an input/output without the Arduino API, and explore how to read/write data in it. Then you can try to go to more complicated stuff, like the ADC, Interruptions, Timers, etc.

Oh and one last note. If you want to program embedded systems, I won't recommend you to begin with micro processors (ARM). Start with micro controllers, as these tend to be simpler and easier. Then, if you want to you can move on to micro processors, although many embedded systems use micro controllers.

Thanks for the advice. I do think that arduino helped me get some fundamentals down. I didn't even have a concept of pull-up / pull-down resistors until breadboarding some circuits with an arduino.

I am now focusing on atmegas and atmel studio and have found the change to C and a full IDE pretty daunting. It took me some practice to get my head around the registers for configuring the micro, and bit operations, but I'm getting there. I'm finding google and Github a huge help. I can find code for almost anything that I can learn from and adapt instead of trying to understand the data sheets alone.

I now have TWI/I2C and SPI working, but I still have lots to learn (inventing a protocol, best practice, etc). In fact I might ask about that in a new thread.

Oh, and the ARM stuff is staying on the shelf for a while!

My last recommendation, stick to a micro controller. You probably have seen how huge the datasheets are, so its better to stay with one until you've covered every single feature of it. Then you will discover how easy is to switch between different micros. They all are configured more or less the same way, and the concepts are the same. If, after you have mastered micro controllers, you want to start playing with ARM, I'd read a little bit about Operating Systems, as these tend to work under an OS, instead of being just an application loaded into the memory. Good luck!
